reason: The sources provide over 15 cross-verified facts across multiple independent sites detailing the discovery, size, hazard assessment, and close 2011 flyby of 2005 YU55.
story: On November 8, 2011, an asteroid measuring roughly 1,300 feet across slipped inside the Moon's orbit, passing just 201,700 miles from Earth. Named 2005 YU55, the city-block-sized space rock was originally flagged on impact risk watchlists. However, radar measurements taken in April 2010 by the Arecibo Observatory cut orbital uncertainties in half, ruling out any collision for at least a century and removing it from NASA's risk tables. That same radar data revealed the asteroid was twice as large as previously estimated. When 2005 YU55 made its closest approach at 23:28 GMT, radar dishes at Goldstone and Arecibo mapped its spherical, boulder-strewn surface in stunning detail. Moving too swiftly for many optical instruments, the carbonaceous asteroid reached 11th magnitude, visible only to skywatchers with telescopes of six inches or larger. It was the closest pass by an asteroid of that size in decades.
angle: When radar astronomers tracked 2005 YU55 in 2010 to confirm whether it might hit Earth, they discovered the asteroid was actually twice as large as previously estimated.

claims.claim: Asteroid 2005 YU55 was discovered on December 28, 2005, by Robert McMillan.
The asteroid measures approximately 400 meters (1,300 feet) in diameter.
2005 YU55 is classified as a potentially hazardous asteroid.
In April 2010, radar observations using the Arecibo telescope reduced uncertainties in the asteroid's orbit by 50 percent.
The April 2010 Arecibo radar tracking eliminated any possibility of 2005 YU55 impacting Earth for at least the next 100 years.
Following the April 2010 radar analysis, 2005 YU55 was removed from NASA's impact risk watch list.
Radar measurements revealed the asteroid was twice as large as astronomers had previously calculated.
On November 8, 2011, 2005 YU55 passed inside the orbit of the Moon at roughly 324,600 to 325,000 kilometers from Earth.
Closest approach to Earth occurred at 23:28 GMT (6:28 p.m. EST) on November 8, 2011.
Both the Arecibo Observatory and NASA's Goldstone radar facilities tracked 2005 YU55 during its flyby.
Radar imaging demonstrated that 2005 YU55 has a nearly spherical or spheroidal shape.
Spectroscopy and physical analysis confirmed that 2005 YU55 is a carbon-rich C-type asteroid.
The asteroid reached approximately apparent magnitude 11 during the flyby encounter.
Visual observers required a telescope with an aperture of at least 6 inches (15 cm) to detect the asteroid.
The Herschel Space Observatory made far-infrared observations of 2005 YU55 to help evaluate its temperature and composition.
An asteroid as large as 2005 YU55 will not pass this close to Earth again until 2028.

disputed: Rotation period: S1 reports an optical spin period of about 19.3 hours, whereas S7 reports an 18-hour rotation period. A script should state the rotation period is approximately 18 to 19 hours or attribute the specific figures.

Orbit period around the Sun: S3 states an orbital period of 1.22 years, while S4 states it makes a lap around the Sun every 15 months. Since 1.22 years is roughly 14.6 months, a script can describe the period as roughly 15 months or 1.2 years.
